Note::NlpAccessor::to_ascii¶

Back to Note NLP Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::NlpAccessor::to_ascii() const

Force Text Down To Plain ASCII¶

to_ascii() rewrites each cell so it contains only 7-bit ASCII: it folds the accented Latin letters to their base form and replaces anything it cannot represent with a literal ?. Use it when a downstream consumer — a legacy identifier scheme, a filename rule, a fixed-width field — accepts only ASCII and an approximate rendering is better than a hard failure.

How it folds¶

  1. First the cell runs through the same accent fold as strip_accents: a precomposed Latin-1 letter (é, ñ, Ø, Æ) becomes its base (e, n, O, AE), and a standalone combining diacritic is dropped.

  2. Then every remaining byte with the high bit set (≥ 0x80) is replaced by one ? per byte.

Step 1 only knows the Latin-1 block, so a letter from Latin Extended-A (ā, ĥ, ǔ) survives step 1 unchanged and is turned into ?? (two bytes, two question marks) by step 2. To widen the fold, decompose first: to_nfd().nlp().to_ascii() splits ā into a + a combining macron, and step 1 drops the macron — so the result is a. That still cannot rescue a non-Latin script; use to_greek / to_cyrillic for those.

The operation is shape-preserving and cell-independent, works on UTF-8 text (a bytes-mode Note is rejected with Note::NlpAccessor::to_ascii requires a UTF-8 text Note (not bytes)), and returns a fresh UTF-8 Note. A cell that is already ASCII is returned unchanged.

Latin transliteration is the ASCII fold performed by this method. There is no second Latin-specific spelling because it would describe the same operation.

Example 1: Latin-1 Accents Fold To Their Base¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"café", "señor", "Ærø", "naïve"}).nlp().to_ascii())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["cafe", "senor", "AEro", "naive"]

Example 2: Beyond Latin-1 Becomes ?¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"ĥ", "Œuvre", "π ≈ 3"}).nlp().to_ascii())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["??", "OEuvre", "?? ??? 3"]

Œ is in the Latin-1 range so it folds to OE; ĥ (Latin Extended-A), the Greek π, and the ≈ sign are each two or three high bytes and become that many ?.

Example 3: Decompose First To Widen The Fold¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"ā", "ǔ", "Ω"}).to_nfd().nlp().to_ascii())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["a", "u", "??"]

ā and ǔ decompose to a base letter plus a combining mark, which the accent fold then removes. Ω is a Greek letter, not an accented Latin one — NFD does not change it, so it still becomes ??.

Example 4: Already-ASCII And Higher-Rank Input¶

std::cout << pluss::make_note({"plain text 123"}).nlp().to_ascii() << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({{"àb", "c"}}).nlp().to_ascii())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
["plain text 123"]
Note(shape=[1, 2], dim=2, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["ab", "c"]
]

See Also¶

  • Note::strip_accents: fold accents but keep the text as UTF-8 (no ? substitution).

  • Note::to_ascii: the plain cleanup that replaces non-ASCII with ? without the accent fold.

  • Note::NlpAccessor::to_greek / Note::NlpAccessor::to_cyrillic: romanize a non-Latin script.

  • Note::to_latin1_lossy: keep the Latin-1 characters as bytes instead of folding to ASCII.
